190.text: Full measurements: measurements in multi-qubit bases Consider a system consisting of qubits. The wave function of such a system belongs to a vector space of dimension . 274.title: Random number generation
274.heading: Quantum Random Number Generation Tutorial
274.text: Quantum Random Number Generation Tutorial True random number generation is a notoriously difficult problem. Many "random" generators today are actually pseudo-random, using a starting seed to spawning seemingly-random numbers that are actually a repeatable function of that seed. Most true random number generations are based on measurements of some natural phenomenon, such as atmospheric noise or atomic decay. (You can read more about it here.) Quantum random number generators (QRNGs) are truly random. Of course, this only applies to the case when they're running on a real quantum device, relying on the randomness of the quantum state collapse during measurement to produce the random numbers.

However, in "black box" testing the tester doesn't have access to the details of the function implementation, but only to the "box" that takes an input and produces the corresponding output. 642.text: BB84 protocol loops through the two main steps until Alice and Bob have as much key as they want. The first step is to use the quantum channel, where Alice prepares individual qubits and then sends them to Bob to be measured. The second step is entirely classical post-processing and communication that takes the measurement results from the quantum step and extracts a classical, random bit string Alice and Bob can use. Let's start by looking at how Alice will prepare her qubits for sending to Bob as a part of the quantum phase of the BB84 protocol.
